I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I am p4 with $406 and the opponent is p2 with $323. Both are on INCOME_TAX. I own a light blue monopoly with 4 houses on each property plus unmortgaged properties. The opponent owns an orange monopoly with 4 houses and dark blue with 3 houses.

The opponent also owns Kentucky, Illinois, Short Line, and Baltic unmortgaged. The bank has 2 houses and 12 hotels left. I just built one house on Vermont and one on Connecticut. All three light blue properties now have four houses. A $100 payment would force the opponent to mortgage or sell buildings before rolling.

I am weighing whether to build hotels on my light blue properties. A hotel costs $50 plus four houses, and the rent would be much higher than four houses. I also need to avoid trading States Avenue because that would complete the opponent's pink monopoly.

Standard light blue rent values are now clear. Hoteling one property would return four houses to the bank, which would then hold six total. That could let the opponent build more houses on their monopolies.

The opponent cannot afford four houses on both dark blue properties. They have $323 and each house costs $200. Hoteling one light blue property would return four houses to the bank. The opponent could then use those two remaining houses to reach four houses on both dark blues. That would raise the rent on Park Place to $1300.

The opponent can only afford one more house on their dark blue properties. Hoteling my light blue properties would return four houses to the bank, but that would burn the $750 St. James survival buffer.

I am reconsidering the hotel strategy. Returning houses to the bank would not remove the opponent's existing houses on their orange monopoly, so the $750 St. James survival buffer concern may not apply.

Hotel rent on the light blue properties would be $550, $550, and $600. The total cost to hotel all three is $150. Returning twelve houses to the bank would leave only two houses available for the opponent.

The housing shortage is the key strategy. If the opponent lands on my light blue properties and must sell houses to pay rent, those houses return to the bank. I could then buy them back. This would prevent the opponent from rebuilding their own houses.

All 32 houses are currently out. The opponent owns 18 and the bank holds 2. Building hotels would return four houses per property to the bank. Those houses would then be available for the opponent to buy or rebuild.

The opponent cannot upgrade their dark blue properties because they lack the cash. Four houses on both cost $400, but they only have $323. If they land on my light blues, they must mortgage or sell houses to pay rent. Orange houses sell for half their purchase price.

The opponent can mortgage Baltic for $30, but St. James and the four houses on Tennessee or New York cannot be mortgaged while buildings are present. Kentucky mortgages for $110 and Illinois for $120.

Short Line mortgages for $100. The opponent can raise enough cash to pay my light blue rent without selling any houses. They have $323 plus $360 in mortgageable properties, giving them $683 total. Connecticut requires $127 more, which they can cover with Kentucky and Baltic. Oriental and Vermont require $77 more, which they can cover with Kentucky alone. All three properties can be paid by mortgaging alone.

Hotel rent would still be manageable. The opponent has $683 total, so they could mortgage enough to cover the $550 or $600 hits without selling any houses. They only roll once per turn anyway.

I am mapping the board positions to plan the next turn. I just paid $200 income tax and built houses. The opponent is on INCOME_TAX and rolls next, then I will roll. I need them to land once and be damaged, then survive their board.

I mapped the full board positions. The opponent rolls from Income Tax next. A roll of 2 lands on my Oriental Avenue for $400. A roll of 4 lands on my Vermont Avenue for $400. A roll of 5 lands on my Connecticut Avenue for $450. A roll of 7 lands on their mortgaged St. Charles Avenue. A roll of 8 lands on their mortgaged Electric Company. A roll of 9 lands on my States Avenue, which is not yet monopolized.

States Avenue is not monopolized, so rent there is only $10. Virginia and Pennsylvania Railroad are both mortgaged, meaning no rent is collected from those squares. The opponent lands on my light blue properties on rolls 2, 4, and 5, which gives a probability of 8/36. If they miss my properties, they may land on safe squares instead. I also need to watch for my own St. James Avenue, which is twelve spaces away and would cost $750 in rent.

I cannot reach the opponent's orange properties from Income Tax. The only dangerous square is St. James, twelve spaces away for $750 rent. Selling all twelve light blue houses would return only $300, leaving me $44 short of the $750 needed.

I am checking mortgage values for the pink and red properties. States Avenue mortgages for $70, while Virginia mortgages for $80. The red set mortgages for $110 each.

I calculated the mortgage values for the remaining properties. Ventnor mortgages for $130, Pacific and North Carolina for $150 each, and Pennsylvania Avenue for $160. If I mortgage both Ventnor and States, I would raise $200. Combined with selling all twelve light blue houses for $300, I would have $906 total. That is enough to survive a $750 hit on St. James and still keep $156. However, I will not sell my houses now because I want to maintain the rent threat. I am weighing whether to mortgage some properties now to build up cash.

I will keep my properties unmortgaged for now. Mortgaging to pay debts is a post-turn action, and the small rents on States and Ventnor are negligible. Unmortgaging green properties would be wasteful without a monopoly, and I will never trade States Avenue because that would complete the opponent's pink set.

I am weighing trade offers to complete my monopolies. The brown set would be weak. The pink set is impossible because the opponent already holds St. Charles and Virginia. A yellow monopoly would be huge, but they own mortgaged Atlantic and Marvin Gardens. A green monopoly would also be huge, since they hold Pennsylvania Avenue. Four railroads would help, yet it would not beat their hotels.

I am reconsidering the hotel strategy. Hotel rent on Connecticut Avenue would be $600, but the opponent has $683 in cash and mortgages. They could pay that hit without selling any houses. Hotels do not strip their houses on a single hit. I need to double-check their mortgage values.

I confirmed the opponent has $683 total. Hotel rent on Connecticut would be $600, leaving them $83. They would not sell houses. Building hotels now would cost $50 and return four houses to the bank. Those houses could then be bought back by the opponent.

Dark blue properties are unreachable from Income Tax on the next roll, so upgrading them would not hurt me this turn. I must watch for later turns when they could move further and land on those squares. If they sell orange houses to pay rent, returning them to the bank lets them rebuild.

The opponent can already afford one house on a dark blue property for $200, leaving them with $123. They have not upgraded yet, but they could do so on their next turn. I cannot stop the two houses already in the bank. Building hotels would add four to twelve more houses to the bank, letting them build even more.

I confirmed that building hotels is a mistake. Returning four houses to the bank would let the opponent mortgage $110 and buy two houses on the dark blues, forcing both to four houses and raising my death rent. I will not sell houses now because that weakens my kill shot. Mortgaging properties now offers no benefit since I already have enough cash to survive the next danger.

Unmortgaging the remaining properties would cost too much for the small rent returns. I will end my turn.
